points: The chapter opens with a parable - a forest fire in the south burning fresh trees and dry trees alike - and Yechezkel pushes back on parables themselves: 'they say of me, is he not just a maker of meshalim?' The people dismissed parables as gimmicky and open to interpretation. Hashem answers with the plain meaning: destruction is coming, and it will burn the tzaddik (the fresh tree) together with the rasha (the dry one).

Why does the tzaddik suffer? Avraham Avinu asked the same question about Sedom. The Radak brings the Gemara's answer, elaborated by the Ramchal: when a decree targets a city or a population, even the righteous within it suffer - sparing individuals from a communal decree would take an extraordinary miracle Hashem may choose not to bring. That is not a failure of justice: ultimate justice comes in Olam HaBa, where the righteous who suffered in this world go straight to their reward.

The pastoral corollary is critical: the suffering we see around us is not necessarily because of a person's own sins. It can be due to the sins of the people they live among, through no fault of their own. We cannot read other people's pain as a verdict on them.

The second parable repeats 'sword, sword, sword,' interchanging the sword of Hashem with the sword of Bavel: Nevuchadnetzar is only Hashem's agent, the same message Yirmiyahu delivered. He thinks he is in charge - casting quiver divination with yes, no and blank arrows, and liver divination - but he is an instrument. Rashi adds that the repetition also includes the sword of Jew against Jew: Yishmael's assassination of Gedalia and the killing of many Jews.

Finally Yechezkel acts out two paths for the king of Bavel - toward Ammon or toward the Jews - and the king walks the path to Yerushalayim: the destruction spoken about for decades is now imminent, and Yechezkel publicly groans and convulses so the people will ask why. From 'remove the crown' a halacha is learned: as part of zeicher l'churban we limit displays of pride and joy - which is why brides do not wear metal or jeweled crowns, only cloth.
